Volume 08 · Chapter 11

Distress, restructuring and governance

Undergraduate Author-reviewed · Prerequisites: v08-c10

By the endCompare restructuring alternatives and their incentive and valuation consequences.

Capability and prerequisites

You can compare liquidation, continuation and refinancing, identify the value and incentives of every claimant, and explain why an attractive economic plan may still need a contractual repair. Use the cash-flow and equity bridge, financing frictions and old-creditor transfers, dated liquidity constraints, and the agreed private-ownership and preferred-claim contract. This chapter teaches its own finite priority calculations; no option-pricing or bankruptcy-law course is assumed.

A business can be worth more alive than dismantled yet have no cash to meet tomorrow's debt maturity. A creditor can receive less than face value and still earn a positive return on a discounted purchase. A debt write-down can repair incentives without creating a single new operating receipt. The task is to separate these statements, then build a plan whose cash, claim values and required approvals all fit.

All businesses, dates, prices, probabilities and agreements below are original fictional inputs. Money is in thousands of currency units, kCU. When shares are used, their counts are thousands and per-share prices are CU. We stipulate enforceable contracts and specify every relevant claim. These assumptions are not a description of the insolvency law, creditor ranking or director duties of any real jurisdiction.

1. Diagnose the problem before choosing the procedure

Cash-flow distress means that available cash and accessible financing cannot meet required payments at the relevant dates. It can arise from a collection delay, a concentrated maturity, a cancelled facility or persistent operating losses. A positive annual cash forecast does not settle whether the firm can pay this week. A default is failure to satisfy a contractual requirement; a covenant breach can occur even before a missed payment.

Negative book equity means recorded liabilities exceed recorded assets. The conclusion depends on the accounting measurements and is not itself a current liquidation valuation. Economic viability asks whether preserving or adapting the operations yields more value than the available alternatives, after the incremental resources, finance and implementation costs it requires. A useful business may support less than the face amount of its inherited debt. Conversely, positive book equity does not guarantee that operations should continue or that maturing debt is fundable.

Legal insolvency, eligibility for a proceeding and duties near insolvency depend on the applicable legal tests, entity, facts and date. The World Bank's revised 2021 Principles distinguish payment-based and asset/liability tests and recommend clear rules, informed workouts and predictable priorities. They are policy benchmarks, not evidence that a specific local test is satisfied. Our calculations classify the supplied cash and values; they do not issue legal conclusions.

An operational restructuring changes the business: product choices, assets, costs or investment. A financial restructuring changes claims: principal, maturity, interest, collateral, ownership or control. A consensual workout changes contracts by the required agreements; a formal proceeding relies on a jurisdiction's actual authority and safeguards. Liquidation realizes assets and distributes proceeds, but selling a productive business as a unit can differ from selling each machine separately. Specify which sale alternative a quoted value describes.

2. Map assets and claims before building the waterfall

A waterfall applies specified payment priorities to a finite cash pool. It needs the entity that owes the claim, which assets belong to that entity, collateral rights, permitted deductions, any guarantees or recourse, each allowed face amount, and the treatment of the shortfall. A group company's asset is not automatically available to every creditor in the group. A secured label does not promise full recovery when the collateral is inadequate.

For one collateral pool, let C be gross realizable proceeds less its allocated sale cost and S the secured face. Under our contract, the collateral payment is min(C, S), the unsecured deficiency is d = max(S−C, 0), and excess collateral max(C−S, 0) joins the general pool A. Let B and T be bond and trade faces that rank equally with d. The fraction paid per unit of eligible unsecured face is:

ρ = min[1, A/(d+B+T)].
Secured creditor's total receipt = min(C, S) + ρd;
bond receipt = ρB; trade receipt = ρT;
equity receipt = max[A−(d+B+T), 0].

The fraction formula assumes d+B+T > 0. If there are no eligible unsecured claims, no pro-rata rate is needed and the entire general pool goes to equity under this contract. Here A already includes accessible cash, net proceeds of the unencumbered assets and excess collateral. Do not deduct the same sale cost again from the general pool, and do not let the secured creditor claim its full face in that pool after receiving collateral. Equal rank means an equal percentage of allowed face, not an equal number of currency units per creditor. If the contract instead makes a deficiency nonrecourse, d is excluded. Other priority classes require a different waterfall, not an undocumented exception to this one.

Worked example 1 — Brindle's liquidation and investor return

Brindle Ceramics must choose a plan on 1 January 2027, date 0. Immediate liquidation would sell collateral for 70, with sale costs 10 charged only to that pool. Unencumbered assets sell for 45, with separate costs 5. Cash is 10. There are three old debt classes: secured face 90, bonds 45, and trade claims 30. These allowed faces include all contractually included amounts. No taxes, employee claims, leases, guarantees, other expenses or additional creditors are omitted from this deliberately closed case.

The fictional liquidation agreement allocates net collateral first to the secured claim. Its deficiency then ranks equally with bonds and trade claims; any excess collateral joins the general pool. All assets are realized and unpaid claims discharged in the immediate settlement. Thus C = 70−10 = 60, d = 90−60 = 30, A = 45−5+10 = 50, and eligible unsecured face is 30+45+30 = 105. Therefore ρ = 50/105 = 10/21 ≈ 47.6190%.

Brindle's immediate cash recoveries, kCU
Old claimantCollateral cashGeneral-pool cashTotal receiptReceipt / original face
Secured creditor, face 9060100/7520/7 ≈ 74.285752/63 ≈ 82.5397%
Bonds, face 450150/7150/7 ≈ 21.428610/21 ≈ 47.6190%
Trade, face 300100/7100/7 ≈ 14.285710/21 ≈ 47.6190%
Old common equity000Not a debt face ratio

Recoveries sum to 110, matching gross assets and cash 70+45+10 less distinct costs 10+5. The secured creditor receives 60 plus a percentage of its deficiency, not 60 plus a second claim of 90. All three debt classes are impaired relative to face, although their recovery percentages differ.

Suppose an investor bought the entire bond claim for 18 six months earlier, when recovery was uncertain, received no intervening payments and now realizes 150/7. Its holding-period return is (150/7)/18−1 = 4/21 ≈ 19.0476%, despite recovery of only 47.6190% of face. The historical purchase price is not a claim that a known immediate receipt can currently be bought below fair value. With multiple payments, fees or different holding dates, compute the appropriate dated return. Neither face recovery nor a realized distressed-investor return establishes that the issuer created value.

3. Compare net continuation value at the same date

Let X be final cash after all future operating and investment outlays, but before financial claims. Let I be the external money required now after applying internal cash to immediate restart and restructuring costs. A fair new claim is worth I. If all final claims exhaust X, the value left for the old stakeholders under a feasible proposal is P(X)−I, where P prices the dated cash under a stated risk model. Compare that amount with net liquidation value L at the same decision date:

Continuation surplus for the old claims together = P(X) − I − L.

Do not compare gross continuation proceeds with net liquidation proceeds. Do not count new loan proceeds as a benefit while ignoring the new claim. And do not subtract I again after already valuing only the residual left after paying the fairly priced new lender. Internal cash used to fund the plan is no longer a separate cash asset at the final date. A principal haircut changes the division of a given business value; it creates incremental value only through an identified change in costs, incentives or operating choices.

Worked example 2 — Brindle's funded one-year continuation

Brindle can instead pay a restart cost 24 and workout cost 6 immediately. Its cash 10 plus new outside money 20 finances the complete 30; no cash remains immediately after this batch. The restart budget covers the needed interval: there are no further unfunded interim payments. The completed operation produces a certain 154 on 1 January 2028, date 1, net of every subsequent operating, tax, investment and disposal outlay. There are no assets or obligations after the final settlement. The compatible annual return on certain claims is 5%.

A signed unanimous agreement would replace the old collateral arrangement with a new waterfall: new-money lender first; old secured face 90 second; bonds and trade in their 45:30 ratio third; old common equity last. Old faces accrue no additional interest under this agreement, and final shortfalls are discharged. The new priority and standstill are contractual concessions requiring consent, not powers management can simply assert.

The new loan must repay 20×1.05 = 21. It is covered by the certain 154, so the claim prices at 21/1.05 = 20. After repaying it and the old secured 90, 43 remains for bonds and trade. The following table reconciles both future receipts and present values.

Brindle's proposed continuation: date-1 cash and date-0 value
ClaimantFinal cashPresent valueGain versus immediate liquidation
New lender2120Zero NPV after contributing 20
Old secured creditor90600/7 ≈ 85.714380/7 ≈ 11.4286
Old bonds25.8172/7 ≈ 24.571422/7 ≈ 3.1429
Old trade claims17.2344/21 ≈ 16.381044/21 ≈ 2.0952
Old common equity000

Final payments add to 154. Their total present value is 154/1.05 = 440/3 ≈ 146.6667. Subtract the new claim's value 20 to obtain old-claim value 380/3 ≈ 126.6667. Relative to liquidation 110, the surplus is 50/3 ≈ 16.6667. The same result follows from valuing old future receipts 133/1.05. Each old debt class gains under this proposal; old equity remains at zero. These weak participation comparisons support negotiation but do not prove signatures, trustworthy forecasts or actual funding.

Because the immediate funding and rate are fixed here, the certain final cash that just matches liquidation solves X/1.05−20 = 110. Thus X = 136.5 is the total-value boundary. At that boundary, the unmodified priority still gives different classes unequal gains and losses relative to liquidation. A positive or zero total surplus does not automatically make the proposed allocation acceptable to each required signer; Exercise 4 repairs that allocation explicitly.

4. Price risk and ownership changes before declaring a rescue

For risky final cash Xs, a first-priority new loan promising F receives min(F, Xs), not F in every state. Its issue price must equal the value of those actual receipts. In a stated risk-neutral model with probabilities ps and one-period rate r, financing I requires:

I = Σ ps min(F, Xs)/(1+r).

This is a piecewise linear equation: below the lowest cash, all states pay F; once F exceeds a state's cash, that state is capped and only the other states contribute to a higher promise. If even the entire cash stream is worth less than I, no face value can fund the plan on these terms. In a general risky business, use justified state prices or compatible required returns instead; physical probabilities are not automatically valuation weights. Exercise 7 supplies its risk-neutral assumption explicitly and exposes the error from retaining a certainty-priced promise after downside risk changes.

A debt-to-equity conversion replaces specified fixed claims with residual ownership. Its value depends on the remaining business, any prior new-money claim and the new share allocation. If a residual worth R is divided into N new shares, each share is worth R/N under equal rights. Receiving 65% of that residual does not mean recovering 65% of the original debt face. New voting rights can alter later decisions, but they do not create cash merely by being written into a cap table.

For example, a negotiated Brindle alternative could keep the same new loan and final operating cash while cancelling all old debt and common claims in exchange for 100 thousand new common shares distributed only to the old creditors. Their combined value remains 380/3 before any incremental conversion cost. Exercise 5 values a specific allocation and compares it with the priority proposal. Old common owners do not retain an unstated slice after their claims have been cancelled. Consent and the economic consequences of the new control arrangement still need to be established.

5. Close a maturity gap without inventing refinancing

A refinancing replaces a maturing claim with another funded claim. It needs available proceeds now and a credible path to the replacement's repayment. An extension changes when the old claim pays and may change its risk, collateral or priority. Paying 10 a quarter later is not equivalent to paying 10 now at a positive rate. A capitalized interest promise compensates for time only if its actual receipt and risk justify its price.

Worked example 3 — Rillstone's conditional refinancing and consent

Rillstone Services is a separate fictional company. On 1 April 2027, date 0, it has cash 18 and an old note 50 due immediately. It must retain cash 8 through the next quarter; this reserve earns zero and is released at date 1, 1 July 2027. Net operating receipts then are a certain 56, already net of all operating and tax payments. There are no other assets, claims or intermediate cash requirements. The compatible one-quarter rate is 2%.

A new lender commits gross proceeds 32; an independent arranger receives a separate cash issuance fee 2 at date 0. The lender advances the full 32 and receives no share of that fee. Its commitment requires the signed intercreditor agreement. Current funds available for paying old debt, conditional on that agreement, are 18+32−2−8 = 40. The old maturity is 50, so the proposed plan has a 10 maturity gap. A future collection of 56 is not available for today's payment.

Five identical creditors each hold 10 of the old note. The specified amendment requires all five signatures: each receives 8 now and extends 2 for one quarter to a payment of 2.04. Together the old creditors receive 40 now and 10.20 later, worth 40+10.20/1.02 = 50. This matches the value of an immediate payment of 50 under the case's certain cash and enforceable revised rights. The realizable outside option without agreement still needs evidence. The calculation does not mean an actual creditor must accept an extension or that a risky promise should be priced at this rate.

Rillstone's complete sources, uses and maturity settlement, kCU
DateSourcesUses
0: signed agreement and financingOpening cash 18 + new loan 32 = 50Old-note payment 40 + fee 2 + retained reserve 8 = 50
1: final settlementReserve released 8 + net operating receipts 56 = 64New lender 32.64 + extended old note 10.20 + old common owners 21.16 = 64

The new lender receives 32×1.02 = 32.64 before the extended note, and the remaining 21.16 is distributed to old common equity. All debt and cash end at zero. Borrowing 32 and extending 10 do not create 42 of value: both have matched future claims. The fee is a financing outlay to the firm, and delaying use of the zero-yield reserve also has a timing cost. No operating premium is added for the word “refinanced.”

If a required signature is absent, the original amendment and conditional new loan are unexecuted. The calculation above is a proposed funding schedule, not evidence that 32 has arrived. The board cannot report a funded close or invent automatic rollover. It must obtain agreement or specify another available plan with revised payments, priorities and resources.

Now stipulate that one creditor will sign only if it receives an extra 1 at date 1. This is an assumed bargaining demand, not a derived equilibrium strategy. If accepted, current sources and uses remain unchanged; extended old-creditor cash becomes 11.20, new debt still receives 32.64, and old equity receives 20.16. The extra payment transfers 1/1.02 = 50/51 ≈ 0.9804 of value from equity to that creditor. It does not increase final cash or destroy that amount as an operating resource. A separate negotiation fee or delay-induced lost sale would be a different financial cost.

6. Separate participation, coordination and governance

A participation constraint compares a claimant's proposed value with its relevant outside option. A coordination problem arises when a joint improvement needs several parties to act together. A creditor may prefer a plan once everyone signs yet hesitate if it expects others to bear the concessions, disputes the forecast or can demand better terms through a veto. The right outside option is the one actually available under the contracts and circumstances, not automatically full face or the most optimistic sale value.

For a proposal with fixed total old-claim surplus G, transfers among old parties can redistribute G but cannot make every party strictly better off if G is negative. If G is positive, a mutually beneficial allocation may exist, but feasibility still requires the necessary cash dates, permitted transfers and enforceable agreement. A contractual voting rule, standstill, common information room, creditor representative or simultaneous signing condition may address a particular coordination failure. None supplies a universal power to override dissent.

Governance determines who chooses the operating plan, verifies the evidence, controls cash and negotiates concessions. Managers may prefer to preserve positions; residual shareholders may prefer risk that falls on old creditors; secured and unsecured creditors may prefer different asset sales; suppliers may care about future business as well as old claims. Employee, customer and community effects can matter beyond the financial claim totals. Identify material omitted effects and applicable obligations; do not silently count them as zero in a real welfare assessment or invent an unmodeled priority in a numerical exercise.

The 2023 OECD board principles recommend informed oversight of strategy, risk, conflicts and disclosure, with independent judgement. Their stated scope is non-binding and does not replace domestic law. Our proposed process is to disclose interests, obtain a cash and claim register, test independent sale and continuation values, assign review to people without the transaction conflict, record actual consents and funding conditions, and monitor dated implementation triggers. This is a process recommendation, not a claim that following it creates a legal safe harbour.

A useful board memo gives the decision and funding deadline, net alternative values, class recoveries and prices, the new money's actual priority and price, cash headroom, unresolved signatures and the evidence that could reverse the choice. It should distinguish base forecasts from a documented downside and ask whether a related-party transaction, private benefit or selective disclosure is distorting the recommendation. A promise to “maximize stakeholder value” without identifying the affected claims and trade-offs is not an implementation plan.

7. Reproduce the cases and challenge a boundary

Download the original input and contract register, exact standard-library Python lab and execution and benchmark guide. Keep the files together and run python3 v08-c11-analysis.py. An optional argument supplies a different input file. No installation, network or output files are needed; exact rational strings keep all claim sums auditable.

The lab calculates liquidation pools, continuation and conversion values, a separately stated risky revision, and signed/unsigned refinancing proposals. Its deliberately small domain requires a positive face for each of the three old debt classes, so its unsecured denominator is positive. It prices new debt from actual state receipts rather than a promised repayment alone. An unfundable new-money request or a failed maturity schedule has no asserted compliant closing balance. The supplied rates, scenarios and priority rights are inputs, not estimates or legal determinations. The independent checker reconstructs claims and cash, while source and instructional review assess the reasoning separately.

Exercises

  1. Four different diagnoses. In a separate diagnostic snapshot, a firm's recorded assets are 140 and recorded liabilities 165. Accessible cash is 10 against mandatory payments 30 today, with no financing yet committed. A fully funded continuation proposal would leave old claimants value 126.6667, whereas immediate net liquidation gives 110. Calculate book equity and the current funding gap. Explain which observations establish cash-flow distress, negative book equity and a favorable continuation comparison. Can the facts alone determine legal insolvency or establish that the proposal can be executed?
  2. Collateral, deficiency and investment return. A new fictional liquidation has collateral gross proceeds 88 and collateral sale cost 8, other gross proceeds 44 and separate cost 4, and cash 10. Secured face is 100; equal-ranking bonds and trade have faces 60 and 20. Use Brindle's recourse and deficiency rules. Compute every class receipt, recovery fraction and the bond investor's holding-period return if that whole claim was bought earlier for 24 with no interim payments. Then recompute receipts if the secured deficiency is expressly nonrecourse. Reconcile the change to total net value.
  3. Finance a higher workout cost. Keep Brindle's certain final cash 154, restart cost 24, internal cash 10 and 5% annual rate, but raise immediate workout cost from 6 to 10. There is no additional operating benefit. Calculate required new proceeds, the fairly priced senior face, all final claim receipts, total old-claim present value and surplus over liquidation 110. Explain how the extra cost changes old value without counting the new lender's repayment twice.
  4. Aggregate break-even need not satisfy the classes. Under Brindle's original costs and financing terms, derive the smallest certain final cash X that matches liquidation 110 for all old claimants together. At this X, evaluate the unmodified priority proposal and identify which old classes lose relative to liquidation. Find a revised old-secured final payment, with bonds and trade still sharing their remaining pool 45:30, that gives every old class exactly its liquidation value. Reconcile all final cash including the new lender, and state the required contractual change.
  5. Convert debt without inventing value. Return to original Brindle final cash 154 and new lender face 21. A consensual alternative cancels all old debt and old common shares, issuing 100 thousand equal-rights common shares: 65 thousand to the old secured creditor, 21 thousand to bondholders and 14 thousand to trade creditors. There are no incremental conversion fees or changes to operations. Calculate the new share price and each old creditor's value. Compare with the priority proposal and immediate liquidation. Explain what the cap table does and does not prove about value, control and agreement.
  6. Lower refinancing capacity and close the repair. In Rillstone, lower the new lender's gross commitment from 32 to 28; the fee remains 2, all other original inputs remain and no holdout premium applies. Find the required extension, current old-note payment, full maturity payments and old-equity distribution if creditors consent to that extension. Now suppose they permit extension of at most 12. Compute the remaining date-0 cash gap. A separate new common investor can contribute exactly that gap with no extra issuance cost and the same certain 2% one-quarter pricing. Find its fair fraction of the final common residual, and reconcile the cash received by new and old common investors.
  7. Risky new money and participation. Replace Brindle's certain final cash by 18 with probability 1/4 and 174 with probability 3/4, keeping immediate new-money need 20 and all old faces and priority rules. For this exercise, investors are risk-neutral with a 5% annual time return; these physical probabilities therefore also price cash. Solve for the fair first-priority new face, check that it lies between 18 and 174, and compute every class's state cash and present value. Compare promised yield with expected return. Find the old-class gains versus liquidation and assess whether redistribution among those classes can make all weakly better off. How much would a face of only 21 actually raise?
  8. Consent and a board decision. In original Rillstone, one of the five required signers demands an extra 1 at final maturity. Quantify its value and who pays it, and distinguish this transfer from an actual fee or lost operating receipt. Give a conditional recommendation and at least four decision-linked evidence checks. Explain how you would address a management conflict or a favored creditor, identify what is still unknown about alternatives, and avoid treating the OECD recommendations or the case's unanimous-signature clause as universal law.
Complete solutions and evaluation criteria

  1. Book equity is 140−165 = −25. The current cash gap is 30−10 = 20 before any available remedy. The first calculation diagnoses negative recorded equity; the second diagnoses inability to meet the stipulated current payments from accessible sources. The continuation comparison gives about 16.6667 more old-claim value than liquidation, conditional on complete funding, forecast validity and the stated costs.

    These are distinct tests. A favorable continuation proposal does not itself deliver the missing cash, and book values need not equal sale or continuation values. Legal insolvency and procedure eligibility require the relevant jurisdiction's tests and facts; none is supplied. Full credit states all four distinctions, preserves the proposal's funding/consent conditions and does not declare a universal director duty from the negative equity number.

  2. Net collateral is 88−8 = 80, so the deficiency is 20. The general pool is 44−4+10 = 50. Eligible unsecured face is 20+60+20 = 100, giving ρ = 1/2. Secured recovery is 80+20/2 = 90, bonds receive 30, trade receives 10 and equity zero. Their sum 130 equals 88+44+10−8−4. Recovery fractions are 90%, 50% and 50%. The bond investor's return is 30/24−1 = 25%, a holding-period return on the purchase price.

    With the explicitly nonrecourse deficiency, the secured creditor receives only 80; the general pool 50 is divided over bond/trade face 80. Their recovery fraction is 5/8, giving bonds 37.5 and trade 12.5. Relative to recourse, the changes are −10, +7.5 and +2.5, summing to zero. Net resources remain 130; the changed contract reallocates them. Applying either rule without specifying recourse would be incomplete.

  3. Immediate uses are 24+10 = 34, financed by internal cash 10 and new proceeds 24. The certain new face is 24×1.05 = 25.20. Remaining cash after that loan and old secured 90 is 154−25.20−90 = 38.80. Bonds receive 38.8×45/75 = 23.28; trade receives 15.52; old equity receives zero. Check 25.2+90+23.28+15.52 = 154.

    The present value of old receipts is (154−25.2)/1.05 = 368/3 ≈ 122.6667. Equivalently, 154/1.05−24 gives the same result. Surplus over liquidation is 38/3 ≈ 12.6667. Old value falls by exactly 4 from 380/3 because the extra immediate outlay has no offsetting operating benefit and the additional new claim is priced fairly. Subtracting the loan repayment again from the already calculated old residual would double count it.

  4. Solving X/1.05−20 = 110 gives X = 136.5. The original priority pays the new lender 21, old secured 90, and a pool 25.5 to bonds and trade. Bonds receive 15.3, worth 102/7 ≈ 14.5714; trade receives 10.2, worth 68/7 ≈ 9.7143. Old secured value is 600/7, above its liquidation 520/7, but bonds lose 48/7 and trade loses 32/7. The old-secured gain 80/7 exactly offsets these losses.

    To preserve each liquidation value at the later date, pay old secured (520/7)×1.05 = 78, bonds (150/7)×1.05 = 22.5 and trade (100/7)×1.05 = 15. New lender 21 plus 78+22.5+15 equals 136.5. Bonds and trade retain the required 45:30 ratio. A signed amendment must reduce the old-secured final entitlement from 90 to 78 and allocate the released 12 to the unsecured pool. This is a distributional repair at total break-even, not new operating value; weak indifference still does not establish actual consent.

  5. After the new lender, the common residual is a certain 133, worth 380/3. Dividing by 100 thousand shares gives price 19/15 ≈ 1.2667 CU. The old secured creditor's 65 thousand shares are worth 247/3 ≈ 82.3333; bonds' 21 thousand are worth 133/5 = 26.6; trade's 14 thousand are worth 266/15 ≈ 17.7333. Their sum remains 380/3; old common owners receive zero under the stipulated cancellation.

    Against the priority proposal, secured value falls by 71/21 ≈ 3.3810, while bonds gain 71/35 ≈ 2.0286 and trade gains 142/105 ≈ 1.3524. The changes sum to zero. Against immediate liquidation, all three still gain: 169/21, 181/35 and 362/105, totaling 50/3. These values follow equal share rights and fixed cash. The allocation changes residual and voting ownership; it does not prove a productivity gain, appropriate future governance or consent to the redistribution. A debt balance disappearing from the accounts is not an independent valuation benefit.

  6. Current old-note payment is 18+28−2−8 = 36, so the extension must be 14. At date 1, new debt receives 28×1.02 = 28.56 and extended old debt receives 14×1.02 = 14.28. With cash 8+56 = 64, old equity receives 21.16. The smaller new loan is offset by more fairly compensated old debt extension; total future debt remains 42.84.

    If extension is capped at 12, the old creditors need 38 now, requiring 38+2+8 = 48 against cash plus loan 18+28 = 46. The gap is 2. The new common investor supplies it; date-0 sources and uses both equal 48. Final new debt is 28.56 and extended old debt is 12.24, leaving common cash 23.20.

    A contribution 2 must buy a certain receipt 2×1.02 = 2.04. The new fraction is 2.04/23.20 = 51/580 ≈ 8.7931%. Old common owners receive 23.20−2.04 = 21.16, as before. Check 28.56+12.24+2.04+21.16 = 64 and the old creditors' value 38+12.24/1.02 = 50. The larger total common residual includes a new investor's claim; it is not all an old-owner gain.

  7. For 18 < F < 174, the new lender receives 18 in the low state and F in the high state. Fair pricing requires [18/4+3F/4]/1.05 = 20. Thus F = 22, which lies in the assumed interval. Low-state cash goes entirely to the new lender: (new, secured, bonds, trade, equity) = (18, 0, 0, 0, 0). High-state cash is (22, 90, 37.2, 24.8, 0), summing to 174.

    Present values are new lender 20, old secured 450/7 ≈ 64.2857, bonds 186/7 ≈ 26.5714, trade 124/7 ≈ 17.7143 and old equity zero. Expected new-lender receipt is 18/4+3×22/4 = 21, so expected return is 21/20−1 = 5%. Promised yield is 22/20−1 = 10%; the higher promise compensates for the default shortfall in this risk-neutral model.

    Total old value is 760/7 ≈ 108.5714, below liquidation by 10/7. The secured creditor loses 10; bonds gain 36/7 and trade gains 24/7. Their combined gains 60/7 are less than the secured loss 70/7. Transfers among old claimants therefore cannot make everyone weakly better off while preserving this fixed plan and fair new finance. Face 21 would instead raise [18/4+3×21/4]/1.05 = 135/7 ≈ 19.2857, leaving an immediate funding gap 5/7. Treating that promise as a loan worth 20 would hide both funding and participation failures.

  8. The extra final payment transfers 50/51 ≈ 0.9804 of present value to the demanding creditor. Aggregate old-creditor value rises from 50 to 2600/51 ≈ 50.9804; old-equity final cash falls from 21.16 to 20.16. New lender 32.64 and total final cash 64 are unchanged. A separately incurred fee or lost sale would reduce the financial resources available to the claimants; this payment only reallocates the existing pool.

    A defensible conditional response could approve the payment if the demand is credible, the revised agreement is permitted and funded, and its cost is below the evidenced cost of available alternatives. The problem does not supply a liquidation value, replacement lender or enforceable power to compel a signature, so it does not establish a unique optimal bargaining response. Required evidence checks include verified current cash and the reserve restriction; the timing and enforceability of net receipts 56; the lender's actual commitment, fee, priority and signing conditions; each old creditor's authority and signature; and the cash, delay and claim effects of competing plans. At least four checks must connect to a decision they could change.

    Disclose a manager's or creditor's interest in a related transaction, separate conflicted advocacy from independent review, give relevant parties consistent material information and record the approval and funding conditions. These are proposed governance safeguards, supported by the dated OECD recommendations; actual duties and permitted procedures need the applicable law and contracts. Grade a quantified, evidence-linked recommendation and honest treatment of missing alternatives, not automatic acceptance or rejection of every concession.

Teach-back and delayed check

Teach-back. Explain why Brindle's continuation can preserve value while old debt is impaired, and why preserving aggregate value does not settle consent. Answer: The original continuation leaves old claims worth 380/3 after fairly funding the required new 20, above liquidation 110 but below old face 165. The business can therefore be more valuable continued even though not all promises can be honored. The actual class allocation and each outside option still matter. At final cash 136.5, aggregate old value merely equals liquidation; the original senior priority gives the secured class a gain at unsecured creditors' expense. The revised payments 78, 22.5 and 15 restore their respective liquidation values, subject to a real agreement. A write-down is a changed claim, not a new operating receipt.

Delayed check. A verified sale offer raises Brindle's unencumbered gross liquidation proceeds from 45 to 66, without changing its sale cost, cash, collateral or original continuation. Recompute the liquidation decision. Answer: The general pool rises to 66−5+10 = 71, and ρ becomes 71/105. Secured, bond and trade receipts are 562/7, 213/7 and 142/7, totaling 131. Original old continuation value 380/3 is now lower by 13/3. The certain final continuation cash needed to match this alternative is (131+20)×1.05 = 158.55, above the supplied 154. A previously attractive continuation should be reconsidered when its actual alternative improves; the old recommendation is not a permanent label of viability.

Sources and next step

The scoped sources are the World Bank's revised 2021 insolvency and workout principles and the 2023 OECD board-governance recommendations, read within their non-binding scope. They support the distinctions and review process; they neither supply our original numerical cases nor certify a real plan's enforceability. Priority, recourse, consent, discharge and rates in the examples are expressly stipulated.

Continue to corporate-finance integration to combine valuation, capital allocation and downside funding in one board decision. Later banking, risk and institutional study widens the set of financial contracts and systemic consequences. This chapter provides a complete finite comparison, not a general insolvency-law manual or a promise that every viable firm can be rescued.

Sources and further study

  • World Bank — Principles for Effective Insolvency and Creditor/Debtor Regimes (Revised 2021) — Policy benchmark for distinguishing commencement tests, specifying claim priorities and new financing, and facilitating informed consensual workouts. Numerical waterfalls and all contract terms in this chapter are original fictional assumptions, not assertions of applicable law.
  • OECD — G20/OECD Principles of Corporate Governance 2023, V. The responsibilities of the board — Dated governance recommendations on informed review, risk oversight, conflicts of interest, independent judgement and disclosure; supports the chapter’s proposed decision process rather than a universal fiduciary rule.
  • OECD — G20/OECD Principles of Corporate Governance 2023, About the Principles — Explicitly identifies the Principles as non-binding recommendations that do not replace domestic law, delimiting the board-process reference.
